courses.title: Unit 1 · Wake Up! / Neha's Alarm Clock
courses.note: Unit names follow the Marigold edition; the newer NCERT book 'Santoor' has different units — topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: A poem calling a sleepy child to wake up to a bright morning and a story about a girl who dislikes her alarm clock but learns nature wakes her too: morning routines, time words, simple present tense.
outcomes: Learners can describe morning sounds and sights
Learners can explain the story's idea that nature has its own 'alarm clocks'
Learners can use the simple present tense for routines

scenes.text: The sun was up, birds were singing, but Raju pulled the blanket over his head.
Outside, the whole world was busy and bright, calling him to come and play.

steps.title: Idea of the poem
steps.body: The poet tells a sleepy child that it is morning: the **sun is shining, birds are singing**, flowers are open and everyone is up. Morning is fresh and full of things to enjoy.

steps.title: Solved questions
steps.body:
**Q:** Name two morning sounds. **A:** Birds chirping, the milkman's bell.

**Q:** How does the poet feel about mornings? **A:** Happy and excited — mornings are bright and lively.

scenes.text: Neha hated her loud alarm clock and wished it would disappear.
One morning it stopped — but the birds, the sunlight and the sounds of the day woke her anyway!

steps.title: Understanding
steps.body: The story shows that **nature has its own alarm clocks**: sunlight, birdsong, a rooster's crow, the noises of people starting their day. Our bodies also have a natural rhythm.

steps.title: Solved questions
steps.body:
**Q:** Why did Neha dislike her alarm clock? **A:** It was loud and woke her up.

**Q:** What woke her when the clock stopped? **A:** Natural sounds and light of the morning.

steps.title: Answer tip

scenes.text: 'I wake up at 6. I brush my teeth. I eat breakfast.'
'My sister catches the bus at 7:30.' Things we do every day use the simple present.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body:
Use the **simple present** for habits and routines.
- I/you/we/they **wake** up.
- He/she/it **wakes** up (add **-s**).
- Add **-es** after s, sh, ch, x, o: brush → brush**es**, go → go**es**.
Time words: always, usually, every day, often, never.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
*Neha (wake) at 6.* → Neha **wakes** at 6.
*He (watch) birds.* → He **watches** birds.
*They (go) to school.* → They **go** to school.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *She wake up* ✗ → *She **wakes** up* ✓
- *I wakes* ✗ → *I **wake*** ✓

steps.title: Degrees of comparison
steps.body:
- **Positive**: tall · **Comparative** (two things): tall**er** (than) · **Superlative** (three or more): the tall**est**.
- Spelling: big → bigger → biggest; happy → happier → happiest; nice → nicer → nicest.
- Longer words: beautiful → **more** beautiful → **most** beautiful.
- Irregular: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
*A fir is ___ than a rose (tall).* → **taller**.
*This is the ___ tree in the forest (old).* → **oldest**.
*My drawing is ___ than yours (good).* → **better**.

steps.body:

scenes.text: On sports day children dashed, raced, sprinted and jogged.

steps.title: Movement words
steps.body: The poem celebrates running and uses lively **action words**: **run, race, dash, sprint, jog, hurry, rush, chase**. Each has a slightly different meaning — sprint is very fast for a short distance; jog is slow and steady.

steps.title: Solved questions
steps.body:
**Q:** Difference between jog and sprint? **A:** Jog is slow and steady; sprint is very fast for a short distance.

**Q:** Name two animals that run very fast. **A:** Cheetah, horse.

steps.title: Fact

scenes.text: Mulla Nasruddin was asked to shoot arrows at a target. His first arrow missed badly. 'That was how a soldier shoots!' he said.
The second missed too — 'That's how a courtier shoots!' The third hit the target — 'And THAT was Nasruddin!'

steps.title: The humour
steps.body: Mulla Nasruddin is a famous character in folk tales, known for **wit**. Here he turns his misses into jokes by pretending they were other people's shots, and claims the hit as his own. We laugh because his **excuses are clever and cheeky**.

steps.title: Solved questions
steps.body:
**Q:** How did Nasruddin explain his misses? **A:** He said they showed how others shoot.

**Q:** What quality does he show? **A:** Quick wit (cleverness with words).

steps.title: Think
steps.body: It's funny in a story, but in real life it's better to admit mistakes and practise.

**Q:** Is the story real or fantasy? **A:** Fantasy.

courses.note: Unit names follow the Marigold edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: A poem about overcoming fear of the dark and the true story of Helen Keller, who became deaf and blind as a baby and learnt to read, write and speak with her teacher Anne Sullivan: courage, determination and the simple past tense.

lessons.title: Poem: the dark is not scary

scenes.text: When the lights went out, Arun felt scared of shadows on the wall.
Papa opened the window: the moon and stars were shining. 'The dark is just the night resting.'

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: The poem tells a child that the dark is **gentle** — the same room, the same toys, only without light. Night brings the **moon, stars and rest**. Fear is normal, and it can be faced.

steps.title: Tips for fear of the dark
steps.body:
- Talk about it with family.
- Use a small night light.
- Take slow, deep breaths.
- Remind yourself: things are the same as in daylight.

steps.title: Normal feeling
steps.body: Many children (and adults) feel afraid sometimes. It's okay to ask for help.

steps.title: Her life
steps.body:
- **Helen Keller** became deaf and blind as a baby.
- **Anne Sullivan** taught her by **finger-spelling** letters into her palm.
- Helen learnt to read **Braille**, write and even speak.
- She graduated from college (Radcliffe, 1904), wrote books like *The Story of My Life*, and worked for people with disabilities all over the world.

**Q:** How did Anne Sullivan teach Helen words? **A:** By spelling letters into her hand.

**Q:** What word did Helen first understand at the pump? **A:** Water.

'Things that already happened use the past tense!'

steps.title: Rule
steps.body:
- **Regular** verbs add **-ed**: walk → walked, learn → learned/learnt, play → played; spelling: stop → stopped, try → tried, love → loved.
- **Irregular** verbs change: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, teach → taught, write → wrote, feel → felt, become → became.
- Same form for all subjects: I/he/they **walked**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
*Anne (teach) Helen.* → Anne **taught** Helen.
*Helen (write) books.* → Helen **wrote** books.
*She (try) hard.* → She **tried** hard.

scenes.text: At the zoo, Tara saw the elephant's huge flapping ears and the rabbit's long ones.

steps.title: Ears differ
steps.body: Elephants, rabbits, dogs and cats have **outer ears** we can see. Birds, lizards, snakes, frogs and fish have **no outer ears** — birds have small ear openings hidden by feathers; snakes have no external ear openings and sense vibrations. Elephants also flap their ears to **cool** down.

steps.title: Herd facts
steps.body:
- An elephant **herd** has mostly **females and young ones**.
- It is led by the **oldest female** (the matriarch).
- Young **males leave** the herd when they grow up (around 14–15 years) and live alone or in small groups.
- A herd may have about 10–12 elephants.

- **Mud baths** cool the skin and protect it from sun and insects.
- They use their **trunk** to breathe, smell, drink (suck water and squirt it into the mouth), pick food and greet.

steps.title: Why protect forests
steps.body: Elephants need **large forests** for food and water. When forests are cut, elephants may enter fields and villages, causing danger for both people and elephants. **Elephant corridors** (forest paths between areas) help them move safely. The elephant is India's **National Heritage Animal**.

steps.title: Solved Q&A
steps.body:

scenes.text: A raider crossed the line, chanting 'kabaddi-kabaddi' in one breath.

steps.title: Basic rules
steps.body:
- Two teams, each in its half of the court (usually **7 players** on court per side).
- A **raider** enters the other half, chanting 'kabaddi' without taking a breath, tries to **touch** defenders and return to his/her half.
- Defenders try to **stop** the raider from returning.
- Points: each defender touched who is 'out' gives a point; catching the raider gives the defending team a point.
- Kabaddi needs no costly equipment — just a flat ground.

steps.title: Solved Q&A
steps.body:
**Q:** What must a raider do while raiding? **A:** Keep chanting 'kabaddi' in one breath.

**Q:** Which qualities does kabaddi need? **A:** Strength, speed, breath control, teamwork.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Play on soft ground or mats; no pulling hair or clothes; follow the referee.

steps.title: Facts

steps.title: Cuboid facts
steps.body:
A brick is a **cuboid**.
- **Faces** (flat surfaces): **6** — they are rectangles, opposite faces are equal.
- **Edges** (where two faces meet): **12**.
- **Corners/vertices** (where edges meet): **8**.
A **cube** is a special cuboid with all faces equal squares (like dice).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** How many faces do 3 bricks have in total? 3 × 6 = **18**.

**Example 2:** A brick lies flat. Which face touches the ground? The **largest** face. If it stands on its end, the **smallest** face touches the ground.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the faces you can see (usually 3). A cuboid has **6** faces.
- Mixing edges (12) and corners (8).

steps.title: Why patterns

**Example 2:** A path is 10 bricks long and 3 bricks wide. Bricks = 10 × 3 = **30**.

**Example 1:** 4 cm 7 mm = 40 + 7 = **47 mm**.

steps.title: Using remainders

**Example 2:** 100 bananas among 45 children equally → 2 each (90), **10 left**.

**Example 3:** Buses of 40 seats for 125 people → 3 r 5 → **4 buses**.

steps.title: Duration
steps.body: To find time taken: count **hours** first, then **minutes**. 7:30 → 9:30 is 2 hours; 9:30 → 10:15 is 45 minutes. Total = **2 h 45 min**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Leave 3:40 p.m., arrive 6:10 p.m. → 3:40 → 5:40 (2 h) → 6:10 (30 min) = **2 h 30 min**.

**Example 2:** A bus goes 60 km each hour. In 3 hours: 60 × 3 = **180 km**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: How to read
steps.body:
- The clock has **60 small marks** — one for each minute.
- Each number on the dial = **5 minutes** for the long hand (1 → 5 min, 2 → 10 min… 11 → 55 min).
- Read the **hour** from the short hand (the last number it has passed), then the **minutes** from the long hand.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Short hand between 7 and 8; long hand 3 marks after 4. Minutes = 20 + 3 = 23 → **7:23**.

**Example 2:** Long hand on 11 → 55 minutes. Short hand just before 4 → **3:55**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Two ways to show time
steps.body:
- **a.m.**: midnight to noon (12 at night → 11:59 morning).
- **p.m.**: noon to midnight.
- **24-hour clock**: hours run 00 to 23. For p.m. times (after noon) add 12: 3:00 p.m. = **15:00**; 9:45 p.m. = **21:45**. Midnight = 00:00; noon = 12:00.

steps.title: Time facts

steps.title: Parts of a circle
steps.body:

steps.title: Fractions
steps.body:
A **fraction** names equal parts of a whole.
- **Half (1/2)**: 1 of 2 equal parts.
- **Quarter (1/4)**: 1 of 4 equal parts.
- **Three-quarters (3/4)**: 3 of 4 equal parts.
Top number (**numerator**) = parts taken; bottom number (**denominator**) = equal parts in all. 2 quarters = 1 half.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A chocolate has 4 equal pieces; you eat 3 → **3/4** eaten, **1/4** left.

**Example 2:** Is a shape cut into 2 unequal parts showing halves? **No** — parts must be equal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling unequal pieces 'halves'.
- Thinking 1/4 is bigger than 1/2 because 4 > 2. More parts → each part is **smaller**.

- Forgetting a 0 in the quotient (e.g., 412 ÷ 4 = 103, not 13).

steps.title: Perimeter
steps.body: **Perimeter** is the total length of the **boundary** of a closed shape — the distance all the way around. Add the lengths of **all sides**. Unit: cm, m, km.

steps.title: Solved examples

**Example 2:** A field with sides 30 m, 20 m, 30 m, 20 m → **100 m**.

**Example 3:** A five-sided park with each side 12 m → 5 × 12 = **60 m**.

steps.title: Short cuts
steps.body:

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:

**Example 4:** Rectangle perimeter 30 cm, length 9 cm → 2 × (9 + b) = 30 → 9 + b = 15 → b = **6 cm**.

steps.title: Measurement
steps.body:
- 1 cm = 10 mm · 1 m = 100 cm · 1 km = 1000 m
- 1 kg = 1000 g · 1 L = 1000 mL · ₹1 = 100 paise
- 1 min = 60 s · 1 h = 60 min · 1 day = 24 h · year = 365/366 days
- 24-hour clock: p.m. hour + 12.

steps.title: Shapes
steps.body:
- Cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 corners.
- Circle: diameter = 2 × radius.
- Perimeter: rectangle 2 × (l + b); square 4 × side.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body:
- Fractions: 1/2 = ÷ 2; 1/4 = ÷ 4; 3/4 = ÷ 4 × 3.
- Division check: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend.
- Map: real distance = map distance × scale.

steps.title: Top mistakes
steps.body:
- 2 m 5 cm = 205 cm (not 250).
- ₹7.05 ≠ ₹7.5.
- Perimeter: double (l + b).
- Remainder in 'how many buses' → one more bus.
